title: The Sound of a Silent City
text:
When traffic thinned out during public-health restrictions a few years ago, many city dwellers reported hearing birdsong for the first time in years. It is tempting to conclude that the solution to urban noise is simply less of it. Dr. Marta Lindqvist, an acoustic scientist, thinks the matter is considerably more subtle.

In her team's surveys, residents were asked to rate recorded street scenes. Predictably, many of the quietest scenes were popular. Yet some quiet recordings were rated as unpleasant, while a few lively ones, featuring fountains, street musicians and children playing, were rated highly. "What people dislike," Lindqvist says, "is not sound as such but sound they cannot control or explain." A constant engine drone offers no information and no variety; a fountain, by contrast, is a sound that someone has chosen to put there.

This finding has practical consequences. Planners have traditionally relied on barriers and thick windows, which lower decibel levels but do nothing to improve the quality of what remains. Lindqvist's group proposes a different approach, sometimes called soundscape design: adding pleasant sounds, such as running water, to cover unwanted ones, and arranging buildings so that a courtyard is sheltered from the main road. Critics object that this merely hides the problem rather than solving it. Lindqvist concedes the point in part, but replies that cities will never be silent, and that the realistic goal is for residents to feel at ease rather than to hear nothing.

She is also careful not to overstate her results. The surveys involved only a few hundred volunteers, most of them young adults, and people's tastes in sound vary with age and culture. "I would not call this a recipe," she says. "It is a reason to ask people what they actually hear, not just to measure it."

questions.prompt: What is the main point of the passage?
choices: Cities should aim to remove as much noise as possible.

questions.explanation: Cả bài xoay quanh phát hiện rằng độ dễ chịu của âm thanh không chỉ do âm lượng: có bản ghi yên tĩnh bị chê, có bản sôi động được khen.

Sai — Tiếng chim chỉ là chi tiết mở đầu; bài không nói có tranh cãi về việc nó dễ chịu hay không.

title: Why Translation Is Never Neutral
text:
People who have never translated anything often imagine it as a kind of code-breaking: each word in one language has a partner in another, and the translator's job is simply to find the pairs. Anyone who has tried knows that the reality is messier. Take the Portuguese word saudade, which is often described as a longing for something or someone absent. English offers nostalgia, yearning and homesickness, yet none of them quite carries the same weight.

The difficulty is not only vocabulary. Languages disagree about what must be said. In some, a speaker cannot form a sentence about a friend without revealing whether the friend is male or female; in others, the verb must show how the speaker came to know the information, whether by seeing it or merely hearing about it. A translator moving into English must decide whether to add such details, which English does not require, or to leave them out and risk losing something the original author took for granted.

Consequently, every translation is a series of small judgments, and judgments reflect the person making them. A translator who prizes faithfulness to the original may produce sentences that feel stiff to an English reader. One who prizes fluency may smooth away the very oddities that gave the original its flavor. Neither approach is wrong, but neither is neutral. Indeed, when two skilled translators render the same poem, the results can differ so much that readers might suspect they were working from different texts.

None of this should discourage us from reading works in translation; without it, most of us would be limited to the literature of a single language. It should, however, make us a little humbler. When we say that we have read a foreign novel, what we have really read is one person's careful, imperfect interpretation of it. Recognizing that does not diminish the experience. If anything, it invites us to treat the translator as a co-author, whose name deserves a place on the cover.

title: The Case for Slow Science
text:
Scientific journals reward novelty. A study that overturns an accepted idea is likely to be published, praised and reported in the news; a study that merely confirms an earlier result, however carefully, often struggles to find a home. This preference seems harmless until one considers its consequences. Researchers, knowing what is rewarded, may hurry toward surprising findings, and a surprising finding is, statistically speaking, more likely to be a fluke than an unsurprising one.

The remedy, some scientists argue, is to slow down. Raj Menon, a biologist who has become an outspoken advocate of what he calls slow science, says that the profession celebrates the wrong moment. "We celebrate the instant of discovery and forget the long, dull stretch that comes afterward," he says. "But that dull stretch is where science actually happens: someone else repeats the experiment, gets a slightly different answer, and the two sides work out why." In his own laboratory, no result is submitted for publication until a second member of the team has reproduced it independently. This policy has, he admits, reduced the number of papers the group produces each year by roughly a third.

Not everyone is convinced. Critics point out that young researchers are judged largely by how many papers they publish, so a laboratory that publishes less may find it harder to attract funding and talented students. Menon does not dismiss this concern. He argues, though, that the system will change only if respected scientists take the first step, and that funders, who are after all paying for reliable knowledge, ought to welcome the shift.

It would be naive to expect journals to abandon their taste for the new overnight. Yet there are signs of movement: a few have begun to set aside space for replication studies, and some now agree to accept a paper before the results are known, judging it solely on the quality of its design. Whether such experiments will spread is uncertain. What seems clear is that science, which prides itself on questioning everything, has been slow to question the way it rewards itself.

title: Numbers Behind the Goal
text:
Interviewer: Many fans picture a sports statistician as someone who records numbers after the match. Is that your job?

Vasquez: That is the old version, and it is still part of it. But the more interesting work happens before the match. We build models that estimate how likely a team is to score from a particular position, then compare that estimate with what actually happened. If a striker keeps missing chances the model considered easy, we ask whether she is simply unlucky or whether something about her technique needs attention. Luck evens out over a season; skill does not.

Interviewer: Do coaches welcome this?

Vasquez: Some do, some are politely skeptical, and I do not blame the skeptics. A coach has watched thousands of hours of play and has instincts that no spreadsheet can reproduce. My first rule is never to present a number as if it were an order. I say, "Here is something you might not have noticed," and then I let the coach decide whether it matters. The best partnerships I have seen are ones in which each side is slightly wary of the other.

Interviewer: Is there a danger in trusting numbers too much?

Vasquez: A serious one. Numbers measure what is easy to count, and the easy-to-count things are not always the important ones. A defender who prevents a goal by standing in exactly the right place leaves no mark in the statistics, because nothing happened. Her work is invisible unless you know what to look for. So when a young analyst tells me a player is useless because he hardly appears in the data, I ask them to watch the match again, following only that player.

Interviewer: What advice would you give to a student who loves both sport and mathematics?

Vasquez: Learn to explain your results to someone who does not care about mathematics. If you cannot, your analysis, however clever, will never leave your computer.

To record the final score of each match

To judge whether a player's misses come from bad luck or from something that can be improved

title: Soil: The Living Skin of the Planet
text:
To most of us, soil is simply what lies beneath our shoes. Yet a single spoonful of healthy earth can contain billions of microscopic organisms, and the ground is better understood as a community than as a heap of crushed rock. Bacteria and fungi break down fallen leaves and dead roots, releasing nutrients that plants can absorb. Earthworms tunnel through the ground, allowing air and water to move downward. Fungal threads, far thinner than a hair, attach themselves to the roots of many plants and exchange minerals for sugars, effectively extending the reach of the plant.

Forming soil takes an extraordinarily long time. Rock is broken down by wind, water and changes in temperature, and by the slow work of living things; the process can take centuries to produce even a thin fertile layer. Losing it, by contrast, can happen in a single season. When forests are cleared or fields are left bare, heavy rain can wash away the upper layer, which is exactly the richest part.

Farmers who plant cover crops between harvests, or who avoid turning the soil more than necessary, can reduce this loss considerably. These methods are not new; many were abandoned when cheap fertilizers made it seem unnecessary to care for the soil itself. Fertilizer, however, supplies only a few nutrients. It does not rebuild the structure or the living community that make soil resilient.

Scientists increasingly regard soil as a resource that is renewable only in theory. Because replacement is so slow, a field that is damaged today will, for practical purposes, remain damaged for the lifetimes of those who farm it. This is why many researchers now argue that protecting soil should rank alongside protecting water and air, even though, unlike a polluted river, a damaged field rarely makes headlines.

title: Grading Without Numbers
text:
At Harbor Hill Middle School, one grade-level team spent a semester doing something many colleagues considered risky: they stopped giving percentage scores on written assignments. Instead, each piece of work came back with a short comment naming one strength and one next step, and students were asked to respond in writing before moving on.

The idea rested on a familiar worry. When a number appears on a returned essay, many students look at it, compare it with a neighbor's, and ignore everything else. The teachers wanted attention to shift from the mark to the work, and they hoped that students would begin to treat feedback as advice to be used rather than as a judgment to be endured. "A grade is a verdict," said Ms. Dana Pruitt, who coordinated the trial. "A comment is a conversation."

The results were mixed, and the team's report is candid about it. Students said they read the feedback more carefully, and teachers noticed that revisions became more substantial: rather than merely correcting spelling, students rewrote entire paragraphs. On the other hand, writing comments took each teacher considerably longer, and several admitted that they could not have kept up the pace beyond one semester. Some parents, meanwhile, complained that they could no longer tell at a glance how their children were doing. A handful of students even confessed that they missed the numbers, which at least told them where they stood.

The team has not concluded that grades should be abolished. Its recommendation is narrower: numbers should be withheld on drafts, where the purpose is improvement, and reserved for final versions, where the purpose is to report. Whether that compromise will satisfy everybody is doubtful, but it has the merit of fitting the workload of a human teacher.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the passage?
choices: To prove that grades should be abolished
To advise parents how to help with homework

title: The Printing Press and the Spread of Ideas
text:
Historians often describe the arrival of the printing press in Europe as a turning point, and in many ways it was. Before the middle of the fifteenth century, every book had to be copied by hand, a process so slow and costly that a library of a few dozen volumes was a considerable treasure. Printing with movable metal type, associated above all with Johannes Gutenberg, changed the arithmetic. Once the letters had been set, many identical pages could be produced in the time a scribe needed for one.

Yet it would be misleading to credit a single invention with transforming a continent. Movable type had been used in East Asia centuries earlier, and its effects there were not the same. Some historians suggest that the reason lies partly in the writing systems: an alphabet of a few dozen letters suits movable type far better than a script of thousands of characters. Others stress economic factors, such as the growth of towns, merchants and universities, whose members were eager to buy books.

What printing undoubtedly did was make both errors and ideas travel faster. A mistake in a handwritten copy usually stayed local; a mistake in a printed edition could be reproduced a thousand times. By the same token, a new argument could reach readers in distant cities within weeks. Authorities soon realized this, and many responded with licensing rules and lists of forbidden books, which suggests that they, at least, did not doubt the power of the new technology.

The lesson may be that technologies rarely act alone. They amplify tendencies already present in a society, and the same tool can produce quite different results in different hands. It is a lesson worth remembering whenever we are told that some new device will, by itself, change everything.

title: Robots on the Sidewalk
text:
Last autumn, the town of Larkfield allowed a small fleet of delivery robots, each about the size of a cooler, to roll along its sidewalks carrying groceries and parcels. The town council described the project as an experiment. Its reasoning was straightforward: Larkfield has an aging population, and many residents find it hard to carry heavy bags. A robot that delivers shopping for a small fee seemed an elegant answer.

Early reports were encouraging. Customers praised the convenience, and the robots, programmed to stop whenever anything blocked their path, caused no injuries. Complaints, however, soon followed. The machines moved slowly, and pedestrians sometimes found themselves stepping into the road to get around one that had halted. Wheelchair users reported that the robots occasionally stopped in places that blocked the curb ramps. A group of local teenagers discovered that a robot could be paralyzed simply by standing in front of it, and they treated this as a game.

Shop owners were divided. Those with delivery services welcomed the robots, while the owner of a family-run bakery worried that customers who ordered online would no longer visit in person. "Half of what I sell is conversation," she said. "You cannot deliver that in a box."

What interests researchers is less the technology than the behavior it provokes. Dr. Samir Haddad, who has studied the project, observes that people quickly started to treat the robots like unusual pets: some greeted them, others spoke to them as they passed, and few seemed afraid. "We designed the machines for the sidewalk," he says, "but we forgot that the sidewalk is a social space, with its own unwritten rules."

The council has not yet decided whether to extend the trial. A decision is expected after a public meeting, to which residents with objections have been specifically invited.

title: What a Conductor Actually Does
text:
To an outsider, an orchestral conductor can seem to be doing very little. The musicians already have their notes in front of them; the conductor makes no sound; and some members of the audience cheerfully suspect that all the waving is for show. The truth is more interesting.

A well-rehearsed group of four players, such as a string quartet, can keep time by listening to one another. An orchestra of eighty cannot. The players at the back are physically far from those at the front, and sound takes time to travel; if each musician waited to hear the others, the music would drag. The conductor solves the problem by giving a single, visible beat that everyone can follow, a fraction ahead of the sound itself.

Yet keeping time is the least of the job. Most of a conductor's influence is exerted before the concert, in rehearsal, where decisions about balance, tempo and mood are made. A score does not say exactly how quiet "quiet" is, or how long a pause should last; those questions have to be answered by someone, and the answers shape the whole performance. Two conductors leading the same orchestra in the same piece can leave listeners arguing afterward over which of them played the real music.

Conductors also work as psychologists. A good one must correct dozens of musicians without humiliating any of them, and must sense when to insist and when to trust. The famous tyrants of the podium, who shouted and threw batons, are now remembered more for their tempers than for their music, and many orchestras today favor leaders who inspire rather than intimidate.

So the common suspicion is half right. In the moment of performance, the conductor's hands may produce no sound at all. But by then, most of the real work has been done.

title: Farming on the Roof
text:
Across several large cities, flat rooftops that once held nothing more than water tanks and antennas are being turned into vegetable gardens. Supporters of rooftop farming make bold claims: fresher food, cooler buildings, less pollution from transport. How many of these claims hold up?

The cooling benefit is the best supported. A layer of soil and plants absorbs sunlight that would otherwise heat a dark roof, and the evaporation of water from leaves has a further cooling effect. Buildings beneath such roofs generally need less air-conditioning in summer, and the layer also slows the runoff of rainwater, easing the pressure on drains during storms.

The food claims are more modest. A rooftop cannot feed a city; even if every suitable roof were planted, the harvest would supply only a small proportion of what the population eats. The crops grown, moreover, tend to be leafy greens and herbs, which are valuable but light, so the effect on the total distance food travels is small. Rooftop farmers themselves rarely claim otherwise. Mia Torres, who runs a vegetable garden on top of a school, says its real value is educational. "Children who have grown a tomato," she says, "are far more curious about where the rest of their dinner comes from."

There are obstacles, too. Roofs must be strong enough to bear the weight of wet soil, and many older buildings are not; strengthening them can cost more than the garden would ever earn. Water must be carried upward, and wind can dry and damage the plants. For these reasons, most successful projects are on new buildings designed with gardens in mind.

The sensible conclusion, then, is neither enthusiasm nor dismissal. Rooftop farming is a useful addition to a city, valuable chiefly for what it does for buildings and for people's attitudes, rather than a revolution in how cities eat.

title: Inside the Marathon Runner's Mind
text:
Long-distance runners speak of "hitting the wall", the moment late in a marathon when the legs turn heavy and every step seems to require a decision. Physiologists explain part of it: the body's stored carbohydrate runs low, and the muscles must switch to a slower fuel. Yet physiology alone does not explain why two runners of similar fitness, reaching the same point in the same race, can react so differently.

Sports psychologists have long been interested in that difference. One finding is that runners who concentrate on the sensations of their bodies, such as the burning in the thighs or the tightness of the breath, tend to feel the effort more keenly than those who direct their attention outward, toward the road, the scenery or a simple counting game. Experienced athletes often alternate between the two: they pay close attention to the body in order to avoid injury, then deliberately look away when the discomfort threatens to overwhelm them.

Another strategy concerns the way a race is divided. Instead of thinking of the entire distance, many runners learn to think only of the next lamp-post or the next water station. The finish line, which is far too distant to be a useful goal, is mentally set aside. Coaches describe this as shrinking the problem, and the idea applies far beyond sport: a student facing a mountain of revision may find it more manageable to commit to the next thirty minutes.

None of this makes the pain disappear, and the more honest coaches say so. What these techniques change is the runner's relationship with the pain. Discomfort that is noticed, accepted and then set aside is far less likely to end in withdrawal than discomfort that is fought at every step.

title: The Repair Café
text:
On the first Saturday of every month, the community hall in a small town fills with the sound of sewing machines, screwdrivers and cheerful argument. This is a repair café: a place where residents bring broken toasters, torn jackets and wobbly chairs, and volunteers help them mend the objects instead of throwing them away. The service is free, although a jar for donations stands by the door.

The movement began as a response to waste, and its founders' arguments are practical. Many products are now designed in ways that make repair difficult: batteries are glued in, screws have unusual shapes, and spare parts are unavailable or cost almost as much as a replacement. Visitors to the café, however, seem to care about more than money or the environment. "People come in embarrassed," says Joanna Whitlock, a retired electrician who volunteers there, "as if the broken object were their own fault. By the end of the afternoon they are proud."

The learning runs in both directions. Younger volunteers are often better with electronics, while older ones know how to mend cloth and wood, and the café becomes one of the few places where the two groups work side by side as equals. Teenagers who come with a broken headphone sometimes stay for hours, and one or two have become volunteers themselves.

The cafés cannot fix everything. Some devices are sealed so tightly that no amount of skill can open them without damage, and volunteers will not attempt repairs on anything that might be dangerous, such as heaters whose wiring cannot be inspected. They do, though, change how people look at the things they own. An object that you have seen opened up and understood is harder to throw away carelessly.

title: How Memory Rewrites the Past
text:
We tend to think of memory as a kind of recording: an event happens, the brain stores it, and years later we play it back. Research over several decades suggests that this picture is wrong. Remembering is closer to rebuilding than to replaying. Each time we recall an event, we reassemble it from fragments, and in the process the memory can be subtly altered.

Experiments have shown how easily this happens. In a well-known type of study, volunteers watch a short film of a traffic accident and are later asked questions about it. Those asked how fast the cars were going when they smashed into each other tend to give higher estimates than those asked about cars that had bumped. A week later, some of the first group even recall seeing broken glass, although none appeared in the film.

This does not mean that memory is useless. Reconstruction has advantages: it allows us to blend many experiences into general knowledge, so that we know what a restaurant is like without remembering every meal. But it does mean that confidence is a poor guide to accuracy. People can feel entirely certain about a memory that is partly or wholly mistaken, and that certainty is not a sign of dishonesty.

The implications reach into courtrooms and classrooms. Legal systems have begun to treat eyewitness testimony with greater caution, and some teachers encourage students to write down events soon after they happen. For ordinary life, the most useful conclusion may be a gentle one: when two friends remember the same afternoon differently, it is rarely because one of them is lying. More often, each has rebuilt the afternoon in a slightly different way.

title: The Trouble with Prediction
text:
When a weather forecast announces a thirty percent chance of rain and the afternoon stays dry, many people conclude that the forecaster was wrong. When it rains, they conclude the same thing. This is a strange state of affairs, because a probability is not a promise about a single day. A forecaster who says "thirty percent" on many occasions is, if skillful, right when rain falls on roughly three of every ten of those days. A forecast of this kind can be judged only over a long run, and few of us keep that sort of record.

The misunderstanding matters because it shapes how people respond to warnings. Emergency planners know that if residents are told that a storm might strike, some will prepare and others will shrug, and after a false alarm the shrugging group grows. Authorities therefore face an uncomfortable trade-off. Warn too readily, and people stop listening; warn too rarely, and some will be caught unprepared. There is no setting that satisfies everyone, and responsible forecasters are open about it.

Some meteorologists have experimented with new ways of communicating uncertainty, for instance by showing a range of possible storm tracks rather than a single line. This seems to help many people understand the risk, although it also leaves some viewers more confused, and a few complain that the forecaster cannot make up her mind. Whether clarity or comfort is more important is itself a matter on which reasonable people disagree.

Perhaps the deeper lesson concerns our appetite for certainty. We want the future to be announced, not estimated, and we judge those who admit doubt as less competent than those who sound sure. Yet in a world of genuine uncertainty, the confident prediction is the one to be suspicious of; the forecaster who says "probably" may simply be the one telling the truth.
